items.title: Redesigning Workflows for AI
items.summary: A controlled field experiment with 515 startups found that companies achieving the biggest gains from AI didn't use it to speed up individual tasks — they redesigned entire end-to-end workflows, eliminating handoffs and shifting humans to exception-handling roles.
items.why: The headline finding — 90% higher revenue and 40% less capital for teams that reorganized whole workflows vs. task-level AI adoption — is the clearest data point available for any team, including Cuemath's, deciding how deep to actually go with AI.

items.title: Unsung
items.summary: A documentation of Marcin Wichary's redesign of his software-craft micro-blog, which now runs on three typefaces from David Jonathan Ross — Warbler, Bild, and a modified Neonoir — set against a factory-green and white palette.
items.why: Wichary is one of the sharpest writers on software craft (ex-Figma); this entry shows how a complete DJR type system actually gets deployed in practice, making it concrete reference for Manik's editorial typography work.

items.title: I helped shape McLaren's brand. Here's what worries me about the refresh
items.summary: Tom Foulkes, McLaren's former Global Head of Brand, argues that the company's new identity optimizes for luxury appeal at the cost of the enthusiast authenticity that built McLaren's brand equity.
items.why: The tension Foulkes names — premium repositioning that risks losing the community that made you — is a live question at Cuemath too, where brand choices constantly weigh aspirational perception against accessibility for learners and parents.

items.title: Horah Inc lets its love for Pokémon and typography soar in identities for spiced rum, trading cards and book design
items.summary: A profile of Horah Inc, a four-person multidisciplinary studio whose work — from spiced rum packaging to Pokémon-inspired athlete trading cards for On Running and a 30th-anniversary book — is unified by layered vintage typography, bold shape, and pop-culture references.
items.why: The On Running trading card project pulls directly from collectible game aesthetics and applies them to real product and sports branding — a specific reference point for Manik's thinking about belt and XP systems at Cuemath.

items.title: Pretzel Pong minigame in Deel during Oktoberfest
items.summary: Design Spells entry #337: Deel, an HR and payroll platform, embedded a playable Pretzel Pong arcade game into its product interface as a seasonal Oktoberfest interaction.
items.why: A real, shipped example of occasion-based gamification in a serious B2B product — useful reference for Manik's work on when and how to layer playful mechanics into Cuemath's math practice app without them feeling forced.
